tweets.text: Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out. It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend. The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans). More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains. In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries. Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology. I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out. Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) Claude has discovered a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages. Beside the enzyme’s gene sits a long array of repeating DNA—a structure that looks somewhat similar to CRISPR. We don’t yet understand what this system does, but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. But it will take much more work to learn what this system does, and whether it can be put to similar use. 1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here because it really brings out the heart of an important conversation. First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice. I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world. Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people. I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of. But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes. A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice. At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power. This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully. We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors. California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that). More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers. Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up. This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights! Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws). Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers). By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring. BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”. The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure. I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity. This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either. Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker) Sholto, thank you for setting the record straight. Larger issue is that multiple very serious people in Silicon Valley have heard some variation of this and believe it to be true. And the reason it is believable to so many is that it is consistent with Dario’s public messaging and what he outlined in the essay you shared: this technology *might* be dangerous for humans in multiple ways, could lead to extreme concentration of economic power (as outlined in the essay) and therefore needs to be regulated thoughtfully. I agree with the potential risks and I believe Dario makes all of these arguments in good faith. As discussed on the pod, if one agrees that AI *might* be dangerous, there are two ways to address this potential risk. Either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely. Essentially boils down to whether one believes AI is too dangerous to concentrate or too dangerous to distribute. There are reasonable arguments on both sides, but I profoundly agree with Zuckerberg’s statement that: “The notion that AI is so dangerous that the only safe path is an extreme concentration of power seems inherently problematic. Historically, hoping that an absolute power will benevolently provide for humanity if sufficiently enlightened has not led to safe or positive outcomes.” And as Dario says in the aforementioned essay, “some may object that we can simply keep AIs in check with a balance of power between many AI systems, as we do with humans.” I believe this is the best path forward: I want as many AIs as possible to maximize the odds that one shares my own particular values. And as Dario notes, no human has ever been able to take over the world. At this point, I think safe to say that Dario has lost the argument. His messaging has failed to result in his preferred regulatory path. The fact that the only solution to the recent incident where an unreleased advanced OpenAI model hacked Hugging Face was an open-source model likely ended any chance of strict near-term regulation. Essentially every major company other than Anthropic has signed Jensen’s letter. However, Dario’s messaging has been massively helpful to efforts to ban datacenters here in America. I suspect we will see anti-datacenter advocacy groups runnings ads using clips of Dario warning about how dangerous AI could be for humans. His good faith efforts in favor of regulation are now increasing the odds that AI will not be beneficial for Americans and humans everywhere. I believe that there is a reasonable chance AI might help us cure most forms of disease such that we have extended lifespans and can enjoy these long lives in an abundant Star Trek like future. That is the future that I want and I think Dario is decreasing the odds of that future at this point. He is about to be the CEO of one of the most important public companies in the world and given that the pro-regulatory effort has failed (at least for now), I respectfully think he should make an effort to be a more positive advocate for his own industry. And if I am wrong and we do need to regulate this technology, he will be a more effective advocate for this in the future having been open-minded to the alternative. And for the sake of clarity and as I outlined on the pod, I think Anthropic has deep competitive advantages and is an amazing company. Ironically, the main risk I saw to Anthropic a few months ago was nationalization as a result of Dario’s own rhetoric and behavior. — http://nitter.meowing.monster/GavinSBaker/status/2088611616577253502#m

2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI. I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative. In fact it has been about equally balanced between risks and benefits: I’ve written one major essay about each, and even in interviews where I discuss the risks, I make sure to frequently mention the incredible benefits as well as proposing possible solutions to the risks (short clips from my interviews that end up on social media tend to be disproportionately negative, as that gets clicks). In fact, I wrote Machines of Loving Grace because I didn’t feel the AI industry was painting an inspiring enough picture of how the technology could radically transform the world for the better. The bulk of the essay is devoted to refuting skepticism of AI’s potential in health and biology, and showing why I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!). And, if you read my most recent essay (Policy on the AI Exponential), I discuss concrete proposals for how to streamline the FDA process to make sure the deluge of AI-accelerated drugs isn’t slowed down by the regulatory process. I feel the urgency here: I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him. I do agree that the public has a negative view of AI (and that this is a big problem), but I don’t think it is primarily caused by me or any other AI leader warning about AI’s risks. I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust. I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over. The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it. I don’t think that a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin (which some have advocated that Anthropic do) is the way to win back that trust — at this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliche than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*. I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world. That is totally on us, and I think it’s the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing. We are however doing our best to fix this: Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine, and we hope to have incredible results in the coming years and some early glimmers in the coming months. When we’ve actually accomplished something real, the whole world will hear about it, as loudly as possible, you have my word on that. But until then I don’t want to make empty promises, and in the meantime I feel compelled to speak honestly about the very real risks of AI and how to address them. Honesty is the right thing on the merits, and in terms of public credibility and trust it is no worse than, and may in fact be better than, an approach that ignores or distracts from risks which people instinctively understand are real.

In addition to transparency, I now believe frontier models should face mandatory third-party testing for cyber, bio, and autonomy risks—with the power to block or revoke deployment of models that pose catastrophic risk.

6 days and $40,000 of compute with GPT-5.6 Sol to find a critical vulnerability in Chrome, claiming Google’s first full-chain reward in 2026 for a vulnerability that would affect an estimated 1 billion users. Highlights the opportunity for defenders to utilize these tools to secure their software to unprecedented levels: Oege de Moor (@oegerikus) For the second time in Google Chrome’s history, Google awarded a $250,000 bounty for a full-chain exploit… to @XBOW . Here’s the full story: At an all-hands at the start of 2026 in Malta, I set the team a crazy challenge. A full-chain exploit of Chrome by the annual Black Hat cybersecurity conference in August. I believed there were few better tests of whether @XBOW could move beyond web applications to desktop software, servers and devices. Chrome is one of the most hardened pieces of software on the planet, used by more than half the world’s population. A full-chain exploit lets an attacker take total control of a machine, where they can read every email, password and bank login the user types. You don’t need to download anything or click a phishing link. Visiting the wrong site is enough. So @moyix , Andres Luksenberg, Baul Lee, and Willem Pinckaers took on the challenge along with a fifth teammate: OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol. They built a chain they thought would win, but Google told us they already knew one of the bugs. We were already in Las Vegas for Black Hat and DEF CON, and the team didn’t want to go home without the win. So Brendan and the agents built a new exploit in just 6 days. We submitted it to Google and waited. The news came through that we'd done what should’ve been impossible. A full-chain bounty of $250,000, the first awarded under Google’s 2026 rules. It took just 6 days and $40,000 of compute to construct an exploit that affects a billion users of Chrome on Windows. An intelligence-agency veteran told me his team used to spend 6 months on this kind of vulnerability. My takeaway: the cost of finding truly critical vulnerabilities is collapsing, for attackers and defenders alike. Restricting powerful models is not the answer; GPT-5.6 Sol is already public. But defenders have one advantage attackers never will: they can test their own code first. Assume your software is exploitable. Whoever is hunting your bugs has the same building blocks we did. This is cause for urgency but not panic. XBOW is now developing an autonomous product for testing compiled software (desktop applications, servers, embedded devices), and partnering with the world’s top organizations to design that product. Last week, Hurricane Isaias made landfall in the Florida Panhandle. Our thoughts are with everyone affected and with the recovery efforts still underway. Earlier and more accurate forecasting can help protect communities by giving them more time to prepare, and we are grateful that Google’s WeatherNext model was able to assist the @NWSNHC 's expert forecasters. Based on initial evaluations, here's how our model supported the response to #Isaias : - Tracking the Hurricane’s Path: WeatherNext was the most accurate model on the storm’s track. While traditional physics models predicted landfall closer to New Orleans, WeatherNext correctly predicted a path further east. This allowed NHC forecasters to highlight the potential for wind and storm surge impacts in the Florida Panhandle from their very first forecast. - More Time to Prepare: Up to three days before landfall, our model consistently predicted its eventual location in the Florida Panhandle to within 60 km or less, supporting the NHC as they honed in on a track toward the Florida Panhandle and issued hurricane watches and warnings to give officials in Florida, Alabama, and Mississippi more time to prepare. - Early Indications about Intensity: Early on, WeatherNext accurately predicted the intensification to a major hurricane. Alongside the regional hurricane models HWRF and HMON, WeatherNext’s intensity forecasts helped NHC forecasters to predict that the Isaias would approach the coast as a category 2 hurricane from the very first advisory. Giving communities more time and more accurate warnings is critical for protecting lives and livelihoods. While model performance varies from storm to storm, Isaias reflects our broader findings. In our recent @Nature paper co-authored with NHC forecasters, evaluating 200+ global tropical cyclones, we found our model provides ~1 day of additional lead time for both track and intensity. It’s been an honor for the @GoogleDeepMind and @GoogleResearch teams to work alongside NHC forecasters. By combining AI, physics models, satellite data, and the crucial expertise of meteorologists, we're excited to keep pushing the boundaries of forecasting to help protect communities.

highlights.text_fr: Aujourd'hui, nous avons annoncé la découverte, menée par Claude, d'une machine moléculaire qui pourrait représenter un nouveau mécanisme d'édition génique. Sa fonction précise, son utilité biotechnologique (le cas échéant) ou son niveau de signification ne sont pas encore clairs, mais au minimum, c'est un travail dont j'aurais été fier en tant que doctorant. Le travail a été réalisé principalement, mais pas entièrement, par Claude : notre équipe des sciences de la vie a suggéré un vaste domaine de recherche, Claude a lu la littérature et une grande quantité de données génomiques et a découvert quelque chose d'intéressant, puis Claude a proposé des expériences pour vérifier la découverte et notre équipe les a menées à bien. Il est facile de rejeter cela comme un cas isolé ou une curiosité, mais nous avons vu à plusieurs reprises un schéma où la performance de l'IA dans de nouveaux domaines intellectuels passe de faible à surhumaine en quelques années. En 2023, les modèles avaient du mal à faire des maths au niveau d'un lycéen moyen. En 2024, ils ont commencé à bien réussir les concours de maths pour les meilleurs lycéens du pays, en 2025 ils ont commencé à résoudre des problèmes ouverts mineurs, début 2026 des problèmes ouverts plus significatifs, et fin 2026 ils commencent à résoudre les quelques plus grands problèmes ouverts de toutes les mathématiques. Nous pensons que l'IA pour la biologie suit une tendance exponentielle similaire. La principale différence entre la biologie et les mathématiques, bien sûr, est que les mathématiques peuvent être faites purement théoriquement, tandis que la biologie nécessite de l'expérimentation. Certains ont utilisé cela pour en conclure que l'utilité de l'IA en biologie serait limitée. Nous pensons que c'est faux. Comme nous l'avons démontré aujourd'hui, les humains peuvent collaborer avec l'IA pour réaliser les expériences, valider les résultats clés en quelques semaines et, si nécessaire, travailler avec l'IA pour affiner ce qu'ils trouvent. À terme, il pourrait même être possible pour Claude lui-même de réaliser les expériences en toute sécurité en contrôlant de manière autonome l'équipement de laboratoire, avec les protections appropriées, mais nous ne le faisons pas aujourd'hui (notre laboratoire est également une installation BSL1/BSL2 qui ne manipule pas de matériaux dangereux pour les humains). Plus largement, le progrès biomédical comporte de nombreuses étapes — des découvertes fondamentales en biologie à la recherche translationnelle, en passant par la découverte de médicaments, les essais cliniques, et enfin la délivrance effective de médicaments et de soins aux patients. Nous nous intéressons également à ces dernières étapes, mais même le simple fait d'accélérer la première étape des découvertes biologiques fondamentales a le potentiel d'accélérer et d'élargir l'ensemble du processus. Améliorer notre compréhension de la biologie et affûter les outils des biologistes peut faire avancer toutes les étapes ultérieures, par exemple en identifiant de nouvelles cibles médicamenteuses, en trouvant de nouvelles modalités thérapeutiques, en permettant des mesures plus précises et en accélérant la boucle expérimentale qui accélère elle-même davantage notre compréhension de la biologie. Cela n'accélérera pas en soi les délais des essais cliniques, mais si cela réussit, cela pourrait augmenter considérablement le nombre de candidats prometteurs qui entrent dans le processus — une augmentation du débit même si la latence demeure. Dans Machines of Loving Grace, j'ai écrit sur le potentiel de l'IA à "guérir la plupart des maladies en 5 à 10 ans" — un objectif qui semble impossible, mais que je crois juste à peine possible si l'IA est appliquée à chaque étape du processus. La première étape consiste à montrer que l'IA peut d'abord aider, puis mener, les découvertes biologiques. La découverte de Claude est la dernière d'une série de travaux antérieurs connexes qui remontent à des décennies, commençant par des systèmes comme CRISPR, et se poursuivant avec des découvertes comme la recombinase pont et VIPR ces dernières années. Récemment, l'intérêt s'est accru pour les systèmes basés sur les enzymes transcriptase inverse (RT), l'enzyme sous-jacente au système identifié par Claude. Et plus récemment, une équipe de Stanford travaillant indépendamment a décrit un nouveau système RT avec un ensemble non codant associé qui est à certains égards similaire à celui trouvé par Claude, bien que ce soient des systèmes distincts qui ont évolué indépendamment l'un de l'autre. Je crois que nous sommes au tout début de la découverte de tels systèmes et de leur développement en outils puissants pour la biotechnologie. Je suis fier des ressources qu'Anthropic a investies pour accélérer les bénéfices publics de l'IA à travers les sciences de la vie, et nous visons à la fois à faire grandir notre équipe des sciences de la vie et à travailler avec d'autres scientifiques pour étendre cette approche à un large éventail de problèmes. Si vous avez une proposition de collaboration de recherche ou si vous êtes intéressé à rejoindre notre équipe des sciences de la vie, veuillez nous contacter. Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) Claude a découvert un système enzymatique jusqu'alors inconnu caché dans l'ADN des bactériophages. À côté du gène de l'enzyme se trouve un long ensemble d'ADN répétitif — une structure qui ressemble un peu à CRISPR. Nous ne comprenons pas encore ce que fait ce système, mais seule une poignée de systèmes connus partagent ses caractéristiques, et tous sont capables de couper, copier et coller de l'ADN. Historiquement, la découverte de tels systèmes programmables a contribué à révolutionner la médecine. CRISPR, par exemple, est maintenant la base des médicaments génétiques. Mais il faudra beaucoup plus de travail pour savoir ce que fait ce système, et s'il peut être utilisé de manière similaire. En savoir plus : anthropic.com/news/claude-di… Lien Claude découvre un nouveau système enzymatique Dans les premiers résultats de notre nouveau laboratoire de recherche en sciences de la vie, les agents Claude ont trouvé un système enzymatique dont la fonction est encore inconnue. anthropic.com
highlights.text_original: Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out. It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend. The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans). More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains. In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries. Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology. I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out. Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) Claude has discovered a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages. Beside the enzyme’s gene sits a long array of repeating DNA—a structure that looks somewhat similar to CRISPR. We don’t yet understand what this system does, but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. But it will take much more work to learn what this system does, and whether it can be put to similar use. actu.text_fr: Aujourd'hui, nous avons annoncé la découverte, menée par Claude, d'une machine moléculaire qui pourrait représenter un nouveau mécanisme d'édition génique. Sa fonction précise, son utilité biotechnologique (le cas échéant) ou son niveau de signification ne sont pas encore clairs, mais au minimum, c'est un travail dont j'aurais été fier en tant que doctorant. Le travail a été réalisé principalement, mais pas entièrement, par Claude : notre équipe des sciences de la vie a suggéré un vaste domaine de recherche, Claude a lu la littérature et une grande quantité de données génomiques et a découvert quelque chose d'intéressant, puis Claude a proposé des expériences pour vérifier la découverte et notre équipe les a menées à bien. Il est facile de rejeter cela comme un cas isolé ou une curiosité, mais nous avons vu à plusieurs reprises un schéma où la performance de l'IA dans de nouveaux domaines intellectuels passe de faible à surhumaine en quelques années. En 2023, les modèles avaient du mal à faire des maths au niveau d'un lycéen moyen. En 2024, ils ont commencé à bien réussir les concours de maths pour les meilleurs lycéens du pays, en 2025 ils ont commencé à résoudre des problèmes ouverts mineurs, début 2026 des problèmes ouverts plus significatifs, et fin 2026 ils commencent à résoudre les quelques plus grands problèmes ouverts de toutes les mathématiques. Nous pensons que l'IA pour la biologie suit une tendance exponentielle similaire. La principale différence entre la biologie et les mathématiques, bien sûr, est que les mathématiques peuvent être faites purement théoriquement, tandis que la biologie nécessite de l'expérimentation. Certains ont utilisé cela pour en conclure que l'utilité de l'IA en biologie serait limitée. Nous pensons que c'est faux. Comme nous l'avons démontré aujourd'hui, les humains peuvent collaborer avec l'IA pour réaliser les expériences, valider les résultats clés en quelques semaines et, si nécessaire, travailler avec l'IA pour affiner ce qu'ils trouvent. À terme, il pourrait même être possible pour Claude lui-même de réaliser les expériences en toute sécurité en contrôlant de manière autonome l'équipement de laboratoire, avec les protections appropriées, mais nous ne le faisons pas aujourd'hui (notre laboratoire est également une installation BSL1/BSL2 qui ne manipule pas de matériaux dangereux pour les humains). Plus largement, le progrès biomédical comporte de nombreuses étapes — des découvertes fondamentales en biologie à la recherche translationnelle, en passant par la découverte de médicaments, les essais cliniques, et enfin la délivrance effective de médicaments et de soins aux patients. Nous nous intéressons également à ces dernières étapes, mais même le simple fait d'accélérer la première étape des découvertes biologiques fondamentales a le potentiel d'accélérer et d'élargir l'ensemble du processus. Améliorer notre compréhension de la biologie et affûter les outils des biologistes peut faire avancer toutes les étapes ultérieures, par exemple en identifiant de nouvelles cibles médicamenteuses, en trouvant de nouvelles modalités thérapeutiques, en permettant des mesures plus précises et en accélérant la boucle expérimentale qui accélère elle-même davantage notre compréhension de la biologie. Cela n'accélérera pas en soi les délais des essais cliniques, mais si cela réussit, cela pourrait augmenter considérablement le nombre de candidats prometteurs qui entrent dans le processus — une augmentation du débit même si la latence demeure. Dans Machines of Loving Grace, j'ai écrit sur le potentiel de l'IA à "guérir la plupart des maladies en 5 à 10 ans" — un objectif qui semble impossible, mais que je crois juste à peine possible si l'IA est appliquée à chaque étape du processus. La première étape consiste à montrer que l'IA peut d'abord aider, puis mener, les découvertes biologiques. La découverte de Claude est la dernière d'une série de travaux antérieurs connexes qui remontent à des décennies, commençant par des systèmes comme CRISPR, et se poursuivant avec des découvertes comme la recombinase pont et VIPR ces dernières années. Récemment, l'intérêt s'est accru pour les systèmes basés sur les enzymes transcriptase inverse (RT), l'enzyme sous-jacente au système identifié par Claude. Et plus récemment, une équipe de Stanford travaillant indépendamment a décrit un nouveau système RT avec un ensemble non codant associé qui est à certains égards similaire à celui trouvé par Claude, bien que ce soient des systèmes distincts qui ont évolué indépendamment l'un de l'autre. Je crois que nous sommes au tout début de la découverte de tels systèmes et de leur développement en outils puissants pour la biotechnologie. Je suis fier des ressources qu'Anthropic a investies pour accélérer les bénéfices publics de l'IA à travers les sciences de la vie, et nous visons à la fois à faire grandir notre équipe des sciences de la vie et à travailler avec d'autres scientifiques pour étendre cette approche à un large éventail de problèmes. Si vous avez une proposition de collaboration de recherche ou si vous êtes intéressé à rejoindre notre équipe des sciences de la vie, veuillez nous contacter. À côté du gène de l'enzyme se trouve un long ensemble d'ADN répétitif — une structure qui ressemble un peu à CRISPR. Nous ne comprenons pas encore ce que fait ce système, mais seule une poignée de systèmes connus partagent ses caractéristiques, et tous sont capables de couper, copier et coller de l'ADN. Historiquement, la découverte de tels systèmes programmables a contribué à révolutionner la médecine. CRISPR, par exemple, est maintenant la base des médicaments génétiques. Mais il faudra beaucoup plus de travail pour savoir ce que fait ce système, et s'il peut être utilisé de manière similaire. actu.text_original: Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out. It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend. The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans). More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains. In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries. Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology. I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out. Beside the enzyme’s gene sits a long array of repeating DNA—a structure that looks somewhat similar to CRISPR. We don’t yet understand what this system does, but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. But it will take much more work to learn what this system does, and whether it can be put to similar use. actu.text_fr: La semaine dernière, l'ouragan Isaias a touché terre dans le Panhandle de la Floride. Alors que les modèles physiques traditionnels prédisaient un atterrissage plus proche de la Nouvelle-Orléans, WeatherNext a correctement prédit une trajectoire plus à l'est. Cela a permis aux prévisionnistes du NHC de mettre en évidence le potentiel d'impacts du vent et de la onde de tempête dans le Panhandle de la Floride dès leur toute première prévision. - Plus de temps pour se préparer : Jusqu'à trois jours avant l'atterrissage, notre modèle a constamment prédit sa localisation éventuelle dans le Panhandle de la Floride à moins de 60 km, soutenant le NHC alors qu'ils affinaient une trajectoire vers le Panhandle de la Floride et émettaient des veilles et des avertissements d'ouragan pour donner aux autorités de Floride, d'Alabama et du Mississippi plus de temps pour se préparer. - Indications précoces sur l'intensité : Dès le début, WeatherNext a prédit avec précision l'intensification en un ouragan majeur. Donner aux communautés plus de temps et des avertissements plus précis est essentiel pour protéger les vies et les moyens de subsistance. idees.text_fr: 1/2 Merci Gavin pour cet échange particulièrement réfléchi. Je ne passe pas beaucoup de temps sur les médias sociaux d'habitude, mais je voulais m'engager ici car cela met vraiment en lumière le cœur d'une conversation importante. Premièrement, sur la régulation, je pense que 'soit la concentrer entre les mains de quelques entreprises et politiciens choisis via la régulation, soit la distribuer largement' est un faux dilemme. Je sais qu'il y a une sorte de raccourci dans la Silicon Valley où régulation = capture réglementaire = concentration du pouvoir, mais j'ai toujours trouvé cela une image trop simplifiée du monde. Beaucoup de gens en dehors de cette bulle considèrent la régulation comme quelque chose qui contraint le pouvoir des entreprises et profite aux gens ordinaires. Je ne suis pas nécessairement d'accord avec cette perspective non plus, je pense plutôt que c'est compliqué et que cela dépend vraiment de ce que la 'régulation' consiste. Mais en particulier, je pense que ceux qui se trouvent dans le cadre 'régulation = capture réglementaire = concentration du pouvoir' sous-estiment souvent le pouvoir décentralisateur des processus institutionnels objectifs et équitables. Une analogie grossière est que le système judiciaire formel peut parfois sembler guindé et élitiste, mais il défend bien mieux les droits des individus vulnérables que l'alternative, la justice populaire. À leur meilleur, les institutions peuvent conférer du pouvoir aux idées plutôt qu'aux personnes, et ainsi décentraliser ce pouvoir. C'est pourquoi Anthropic a toujours fait ses propositions politiques très soigneusement. Nous nous efforçons de faire des propositions qui désavantagent (ralentissent) les entreprises d'IA de pointe tout en *avantageant* les petits concurrents. La loi SB53 de Californie (que nous avons soutenue), et même la très décriée SB 1047 (sur laquelle nous étions ambivalents), exemptent complètement toute entreprise en dessous d'un certain montant de revenus ou de coûts d'entraînement de modèles d'être couverte (c'était 500M$ pour SB 53, moins pour 1047 mais nous nous y sommes opposés). Plus récemment, le processus de test que nous avons préconisé chez CAISI et à la Maison Blanche implique des tests plus rigoureux pour les modèles de pointe que pour les modèles non de pointe — quelque chose qui avantage différemment les challengers. De même, la lettre 'Pacing the Frontier' envisage (ou du moins l'implémentation préférée d'Anthropic l'envisage) de moduler le rythme des très meilleurs modèles sans contraindre ceux qui rattrapent leur retard. Cela nuit aux intérêts commerciaux des laboratoires de pointe et aide les challengers, y compris les modèles à poids ouverts ! Dans l'ensemble, mon point de vue est que l'IA est *structurellement* une technologie qui tend à concentrer le pouvoir, pour des raisons qui n'ont rien à voir avec la régulation (plus avec les implications extrêmes des lois d'échelle). Les modèles à poids ouverts aident en partie à cela mais sont loin d'être une solution suffisante car ils ne font que déplacer quelque peu la concentration vers ceux qui ont le plus de calcul et de puces (ce sont en gros les laboratoires de pointe plus peut-être les fournisseurs de matériel). Par contraste, je pense que les bonnes 'règles du jeu' peuvent simultanément (a) aborder les risques cyber/bio/d'alignement de l'IA, (b) contraindre institutionnellement le pouvoir des entreprises d'IA de pointe, et (c) laisser de la place aux modèles à poids ouverts tout en abordant les risques spécifiques qu'ils apportent. D'ailleurs, je ne pense pas que les événements des derniers mois n'aient 'pas abouti à [ma] voie réglementaire préférée'. L'approche que l'administration Trump serait en train d'adopter — des tests avant le déploiement pour les modèles de pointe, et aussi des tests des modèles à poids ouverts lorsqu'ils se rapprochent de la pointe — est une que je soutiens très fortement, bien que je doive bien sûr en voir les détails pour en être sûr. Je soutiens également les idées de Demis Hassabis concernant une entité de type FINRA. Cela contraste avec il y a six mois, lorsque la plupart de l'industrie poussait encore à la préemption de toute régulation étatique et à aucune approche fédérale apparente non plus. Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker) Sholto, merci d'avoir remis les pendules à l'heure. Le problème plus large est que de multiples personnes très sérieuses dans la Silicon Valley ont entendu une variation de cela et le croient vrai. Et la raison pour laquelle c'est crédible pour tant de personnes est que c'est cohérent avec le message public de Dario et ce qu'il a exposé dans l'essai que vous avez partagé : cette technologie *pourrait* être dangereuse pour les humains de multiples façons, pourrait conduire à une concentration extrême du pouvoir économique (comme exposé dans l'essai) et donc doit être régulée de manière réfléchie. Je suis d'accord avec les risques potentiels et je crois que Dario formule tous ces arguments de bonne foi. Comme discuté dans le podcast, si l'on est d'accord que l'IA *pourrait* être dangereuse, il y a deux façons d'aborder ce risque potentiel. Soit la concentrer entre les mains de quelques entreprises et politiciens choisis via la régulation, soit la distribuer largement. Essentiellement, cela revient à savoir si l'on croit que l'IA est trop dangereuse pour être concentrée ou trop dangereuse pour être distribuée. Il y a des arguments raisonnables des deux côtés, mais je suis profondément d'accord avec la déclaration de Zuckerberg : 'L'idée que l'IA est si dangereuse que la seule voie sûre est une concentration extrême du pouvoir semble intrinsèquement problématique. Historiquement, espérer qu'un pouvoir absolu pourvoira bénévolement à l'humanité s'il est suffisamment éclairé n'a pas conduit à des résultats sûrs ou positifs.' Et comme le dit Dario dans l'essai susmentionné, 'certains objecteront que nous pouvons simplement contrôler les IA par un équilibre des pouvoirs entre de nombreux systèmes d'IA, comme nous le faisons avec les humains.' Je crois que c'est la meilleure voie à suivre : je veux autant d'IA que possible pour maximiser les chances qu'une d'entre elles partage mes propres valeurs particulières. Et comme le note Dario, aucun humain n'a jamais été capable de prendre le contrôle du monde. À ce point, je pense qu'il est juste de dire que Dario a perdu l'argument. Son message n'a pas abouti à sa voie réglementaire préférée. Le fait que la seule solution à l'incident récent où un modèle OpenAI avancé non publié a piraté Hugging Face était un modèle open-source a probablement mis fin à toute chance de régulation stricte à court terme. Pratiquement toutes les grandes entreprises autres qu'Anthropic ont signé la lettre de Jensen. Cependant, le message de Dario a été massivement utile aux efforts visant à interdire les centres de données ici en Amérique. Je soupçonne que nous verrons des groupes de défense anti-centres de données diffuser des publicités utilisant des extraits de Dario avertissant à quel point l'IA pourrait être dangereuse pour les humains. Ses efforts de bonne foi en faveur de la régulation augmentent maintenant les chances que l'IA ne soit pas bénéfique pour les Américains et les humains partout. Je crois qu'il y a une chance raisonnable que l'IA puisse nous aider à guérir la plupart des formes de maladies de sorte que nous ayons des durées de vie prolongées et puissions profiter de ces longues vies dans un futur abondant de type Star Trek. C'est le futur que je veux et je pense que Dario diminue les chances de ce futur à ce stade. Il est sur le point de devenir le PDG de l'une des entreprises publiques les plus importantes du monde et, étant donné que l'effort pro-réglementaire a échoué (du moins pour l'instant), je pense respectueusement qu'il devrait s'efforcer d'être un défenseur plus positif de sa propre industrie. Et si je me trompe et que nous avons besoin de réguler cette technologie, il sera un défenseur plus efficace à l'avenir, ayant été ouvert à l'alternative.
idees.text_original: 1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here because it really brings out the heart of an important conversation. First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice. I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world. Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people. I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of. But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes. A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice. At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power. This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully. We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors. California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that). More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers. Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up. This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights! Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws). Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers). By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring. BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”. The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure. I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity. This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either. Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker) Sholto, thank you for setting the record straight. Larger issue is that multiple very serious people in Silicon Valley have heard some variation of this and believe it to be true. And the reason it is believable to so many is that it is consistent with Dario’s public messaging and what he outlined in the essay you shared: this technology *might* be dangerous for humans in multiple ways, could lead to extreme concentration of economic power (as outlined in the essay) and therefore needs to be regulated thoughtfully. I agree with the potential risks and I believe Dario makes all of these arguments in good faith. As discussed on the pod, if one agrees that AI *might* be dangerous, there are two ways to address this potential risk. Either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely. Essentially boils down to whether one believes AI is too dangerous to concentrate or too dangerous to distribute. There are reasonable arguments on both sides, but I profoundly agree with Zuckerberg’s statement that: “The notion that AI is so dangerous that the only safe path is an extreme concentration of power seems inherently problematic. Historically, hoping that an absolute power will benevolently provide for humanity if sufficiently enlightened has not led to safe or positive outcomes.” And as Dario says in the aforementioned essay, “some may object that we can simply keep AIs in check with a balance of power between many AI systems, as we do with humans.” I believe this is the best path forward: I want as many AIs as possible to maximize the odds that one shares my own particular values. And as Dario notes, no human has ever been able to take over the world. At this point, I think safe to say that Dario has lost the argument. His messaging has failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path. The fact that the only solution to the recent incident where an unreleased advanced OpenAI model hacked Hugging Face was an open-source model likely ended any chance of strict near-term regulation. Essentially every major company other than Anthropic has signed Jensen’s letter. However, Dario’s messaging has been massively helpful to efforts to ban datacenters here in America. I suspect we will see anti-datacenter advocacy groups runnings ads using clips of Dario warning about how dangerous AI could be for humans. His good faith efforts in favor of regulation are now increasing the odds that AI will not be beneficial for Americans and humans everywhere. I believe that there is a reasonable chance AI might help us cure most forms of disease such that we have extended lifespans and can enjoy these long lives in an abundant Star Trek like future. That is the future that I want and I think Dario is decreasing the odds of that future at this point. He is about to be the CEO of one of the most important public companies in the world and given that the pro-regulatory effort has failed (at least for now), I respectfully think he should make an effort to be a more positive advocate for his own industry. And if I am wrong and we do need to regulate this technology, he will be a more effective advocate for this in the future having been open-minded to the alternative.
idees.decryptage: La "capture réglementaire" est une situation où l'industrie qu'une réglementation est censée contrôler influence ou domine le processus réglementaire à son propre avantage. idees.text_fr: 2/2 Deuxièmement, sur la communication autour de l'IA. Je ne suis pas d'accord pour dire que mon message a été disproportionnellement négatif. En fait, il a été à peu près équilibré entre les risques et les avantages : j'ai écrit un essai majeur sur chacun, et même dans les interviews où je discute des risques, je m'assure de mentionner fréquemment les incroyables avantages ainsi que de proposer des solutions possibles aux risques (les courts extraits de mes interviews qui se retrouvent sur les médias sociaux ont tendance à être disproportionnellement négatifs, car cela génère des clics). En fait, j'ai écrit Machines of Loving Grace parce que je ne sentais pas que l'industrie de l'IA peignait une image suffisamment inspirante de la façon dont la technologie pourrait transformer radicalement le monde pour le mieux. La majeure partie de l'essai est consacrée à réfuter le scepticisme quant au potentiel de l'IA en matière de santé et de biologie, et à montrer pourquoi je pense qu'il sera réellement possible de guérir la plupart des maladies humaines en environ 5 à 10 ans, aussi fou que cela puisse paraître aux gens ordinaires et franchement aussi aux biologistes (j'en étais un !). Et, si vous lisez mon essai le plus récent (Policy on the AI Exponential), je discute de propositions concrètes pour rationaliser le processus de la FDA afin de s'assurer que le déluge de médicaments accélérés par l'IA ne soit pas ralenti par le processus réglementaire. Je ressens l'urgence ici : j'ai perdu mon père à cause de l'hépatite C quelques années seulement avant le développement d'antiviraux à action directe (sofosbuvir), qui guérissent 95% des patients et l'auraient probablement guéri. Je suis d'accord que le public a une vision négative de l'IA (et que c'est un gros problème), mais je ne pense pas que cela soit principalement causé par moi ou par tout autre leader de l'IA avertissant des risques de l'IA. Je pense que c'est fondamentalement une crise de confiance. Je pense que les gens ordinaires ne font pas confiance aux entreprises, aux gouvernements ou à l'industrie technologique et soupçonnent toujours que nous sommes en train de concocter une nouvelle façon de les arnaquer. Les causes de cela remontent à des décennies et l'IA n'en est que la dernière itération. Je ne pense pas qu'une campagne de marketing tape-à-l'œil avec une tournure positive (que certains ont préconisée pour Anthropic) soit la façon de regagner cette confiance — à ce stade, dire que l'IA va guérir le cancer est plus un cliché qu'une source d'inspiration, et la plupart des gens pensent que c'est trompeur. Ce qui fonctionnera, c'est *réellement guérir le cancer*. Je pense que la critique de loin la plus juste des entreprises d'IA, y compris Anthropic, est que nous n'avons pas encore tenu nos grandes promesses de bénéficier au monde. Cela nous incombe entièrement, et je pense que c'est la critique que vous devriez faire, au lieu de tout ce qui concerne la communication et le marketing. Nous faisons cependant de notre mieux pour y remédier : Anthropic intensifie très rapidement ses efforts en biologie et médecine, et nous espérons avoir des résultats incroyables dans les années à venir et quelques premières lueurs dans les mois à venir. Lorsque nous aurons réellement accompli quelque chose de réel, le monde entier en entendra parler, aussi fort que possible, je vous donne ma parole. Mais d'ici là, je ne veux pas faire de fausses promesses, et en attendant, je me sens obligé de parler honnêtement des risques très réels de l'IA et de la façon de les aborder.
idees.text_original: 2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI. I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative. In fact it has been about equally balanced between risks and benefits: I’ve written one major essay about each, and even in interviews where I discuss the risks, I make sure to frequently mention the incredible benefits as well as proposing possible solutions to the risks (short clips from my interviews that end up on social media tend to be disproportionately negative, as that gets clicks). In fact, I wrote Machines of Loving Grace because I didn’t feel the AI industry was painting an inspiring enough picture of how the technology could radically transform the world for the better. The bulk of the essay is devoted to refuting skepticism of AI’s potential in health and biology, and showing why I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!). And, if you read my most recent essay (Policy on the AI Exponential), I discuss concrete proposals for how to streamline the FDA process to make sure the deluge of AI-accelerated drugs isn’t slowed down by the regulatory process. I feel the urgency here: I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him. I do agree that the public has a negative view of AI (and that this is a big problem), but I don’t think it is primarily caused by me or any other AI leader warning about AI’s risks. I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust. I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over. The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it. I don’t think that a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin (which some have advocated that Anthropic do) is the way to win back that trust — at this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliche than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*. I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world. That is totally on us, and I think it’s the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing. We are however doing our best to fix this: Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine, and we hope to have incredible results in the coming years and some early glimmers in the coming months. When we’ve actually accomplished something real, the whole world will hear about it, as loudly as possible, you have my word on that. But until then I don’t want to make empty promises, and in the meantime I feel compelled to speak honestly about the very real risks of AI and how to address them. Honesty is the right thing on the merits, and in terms of public credibility and trust it is no worse than, and may in fact be better than, an approach that ignores or distracts from risks which people instinctively understand are real.

idees.text_fr: Je suis tellement triste. Ce magasin c'est Sat Elite, un magasin de Jeux Vidéos indépendant situé boulevard Voltaire.
